Family Health

Anal cancer: symptoms, diagnosis and treatment options

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Bleeding or a lump near the anus often has a non-cancerous cause, but persistent changes deserve assessment. Anal cancer has established treatments, and understanding the exact diagnosis is the first step toward a useful plan.

What anal cancer is

Anal cancer develops when cells in the anus grow abnormally and become malignant. The anus is the opening through which stool leaves the body; the anal canal connects it to the rectum. Cancer can start in the canal lining or in the skin around the opening. It is less common than cancer of the colon or rectum.

A tumour is a growth, but not every tumour is cancer. Benign growths, precancerous cell changes and invasive cancers are different findings. The exact tissue diagnosis matters because it determines whether treatment, monitoring or reassurance is appropriate. A lump or bleeding cannot be classified accurately from symptoms alone.

Benign growths are not a type of cancer

Polyps, skin tags, warts and some uncommon tumours, such as granular cell tumours, can occur around the anus without being invasive cancer. A skin tag is not automatically a precancer, and a benign diagnosis should not be described as malignant. Conversely, a new lesion should not be assumed benign simply because it looks like a familiar tag.

Some growths contain abnormal areas that need closer assessment. A clinician may recommend sampling a lesion that is uncertain, changing or unusual. The purpose is to identify what it actually is, not to imply that every non-cancerous growth will eventually turn into cancer.

Precancer, AIN and Bowen disease

Anal intraepithelial neoplasia, or AIN, describes abnormal cells limited to the surface lining. Another term is squamous intraepithelial lesion, or SIL. Low-grade and high-grade changes have different implications. High-grade changes deserve specialist assessment because some can progress to invasive cancer; they are not merely another name for an ordinary benign lump.

Bowen disease refers to squamous cell carcinoma in situ in the skin. “In situ” means that the abnormal cells remain in the surface layer rather than invading deeper tissue. Terminology can overlap with high-grade surface changes, so ask the specialist to explain the pathology wording and the recommended treatment or follow-up.

Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type

Squamous cells line much of the anal canal and the skin at its edge. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma starts in these cells and grows beyond the surface layer. It accounts for nearly nine in ten anal cancers in the United States. Most general discussions of anal-cancer treatment refer primarily to this type.

A cancer in the anal canal and a small cancer confined to nearby skin may have different treatment options. The relationship to the sphincter muscles, which help control stool, is important when planning treatment. The team considers the site and extent as well as the name of the cell type.

Less common types: basal cell cancer and adenocarcinoma

Basal cell carcinoma can rarely arise in the skin around the anus. Although this type of skin cancer is much more common on sun-exposed areas, the lack of sun exposure does not rule it out at a perianal site. Its management may differ from that of an anal squamous cancer.

Adenocarcinoma arises from glandular cells, including cells near the upper anal canal or in anal glands. It is uncommon and is often managed along pathways used for rectal adenocarcinoma. Other rare cancers also occur in this region. A pathology report and specialist discussion are needed before applying a treatment plan intended for the usual squamous type.

Cancer that has spread from somewhere else is different

Occasionally, cancer found in or near the anus represents spread or direct extension from another primary cancer. A metastasis retains the identity of the cancer where it began; it does not become a new primary anal cancer just because cells are found there. Tests on the tissue help clinicians work out its origin.

The reverse is also possible: a primary anal cancer can spread to lymph nodes or distant organs. This affects staging and treatment. Ask whether the diagnosis describes a cancer that started in the anus, a nearby cancer extending into it, or metastatic disease, because those terms have different meanings.

Symptoms that deserve a medical appointment

Possible symptoms include bleeding, a lump, pain or pressure near the anus, persistent itching, discharge and a change in bowel habits. Some people notice a change in stool shape or a feeling that emptying is incomplete. None of these symptoms alone proves cancer, and some early cancers cause few noticeable symptoms.

Haemorrhoids, fissures and infections can cause similar problems. Irritable bowel syndrome can alter bowel habits but should not be used to explain rectal bleeding without further assessment. Have a persistent or unexplained change checked. Heavy bleeding or bleeding that will not stop needs emergency help rather than a routine cancer-screening appointment.

Persistent high-risk HPV is the main cause

Human papillomavirus, or HPV, includes many virus types. Persistent infection with certain high-risk types can lead to cell changes and eventually cancer. HPV is associated with most anal squamous cancers, but an HPV infection does not mean that cancer is inevitable. Many infections become undetectable without causing disease.

HPV also remains the main cause of cervical cancer; the introduction of cervical screening did not change that biological relationship. Screening can detect precancerous changes so they can be managed. A previous infection or abnormal screening result is a reason for appropriate follow-up, not a way to predict exactly when or whether cancer will develop.

Other factors that affect risk

Risk is higher in people with HIV and in some people taking medicines that suppress immunity, including after an organ transplant. A history of other HPV-related cancers or precancers can also be relevant. Anal cancer becomes more common with increasing age, but symptoms deserve attention in younger adults too.

Sexual contact can expose someone to HPV, and certain exposure patterns are associated with higher anal-cancer risk. This is not a moral judgement and does not establish how or when an individual acquired HPV. People can develop anal cancer without a history of receptive anal sex. Smoking also increases risk; quitting is beneficial rather than pointless once someone has smoked.

Examination and biopsy establish the diagnosis

A clinician asks about symptoms and health history, then examines the area. With consent, a digital rectal examination uses a lubricated gloved finger to feel for abnormalities. Anoscopy or proctoscopy allows a closer look inside. A rectal examination may occur during another assessment, but should not be assumed to happen at every routine pelvic or prostate visit.

A biopsy removes a small tissue sample for a pathologist to examine. It is usually needed to confirm a suspicious lesion and identify its type. Ultrasound or other imaging can provide additional information. You can ask what will happen during the examination, request a chaperone and tell the clinician if pain requires a different approach.

Anal screening is not the same as a cervical Pap test

Anal cytology collects cells from the anal canal. Cervical cytology collects cells from the cervix; one does not substitute for the other. An abnormal anal screening result can lead to high-resolution anoscopy and biopsy. Screening is intended for people without symptoms in defined risk groups, whereas a new symptom calls for diagnostic assessment.

There is no universal anal-screening programme for all adults. Current US HIV guidance recommends starting a structured programme at age 35 for men who have sex with men and transgender women with HIV, and at age 45 for other people with HIV. Access to high-resolution anoscopy and treatment affects the pathway. Follow the local specialist plan; do not wait for a screening age if symptoms appear.

Staging guides a treatment plan

After a cancer diagnosis, the team assesses the size of the tumour, nearby involvement, lymph nodes and any distant spread. Imaging and other tests are selected for the situation. Stage describes how far the cancer has developed; grade describes how abnormal the cells look. These are separate pieces of information.

Treatment also depends on the cell type, general health, previous treatment and the person’s priorities. A multidisciplinary team can explain the aim: cure, longer-term control, symptom relief or a combination. A second opinion can be useful for a rare tumour or a complicated decision. Bring the pathology report and scans if you seek one.

Chemoradiotherapy is an established treatment

For many anal squamous cancers that have not spread to distant organs, chemotherapy and radiotherapy are given together with the aim of curing the cancer while preserving anal function. This combination is called chemoradiotherapy or chemoradiation. It is incorrect to say that anal cancer has no specific treatment.

Common chemotherapy combinations include mitomycin with fluorouracil, or mitomycin with capecitabine. Some medicines are given into a vein and others as tablets. The exact regimen and radiation schedule are chosen by the oncology team. These examples explain the approach; they are not interchangeable prescriptions or a complete list of options.

Radiotherapy is conventional cancer care

Radiotherapy uses carefully planned high-energy radiation directed at cancer tissue. External-beam treatment comes from a machine outside the body and is commonly used for anal cancer. It can damage nearby healthy cells as well as the tumour, which is why planning, dose and supportive care matter.

It may be combined with chemotherapy or used in selected circumstances to control symptoms. It should not be described as an alternative remedy. Before treatment, ask about the number of visits, care of the skin and bowel symptoms, and whom to contact if side effects make eating, drinking or daily activities difficult.

When local surgery may be suitable

Selected small cancers at the anal margin can sometimes be removed with a local excision, taking the tumour and a rim of surrounding tissue. The surgeon considers whether complete removal is possible without damaging the muscles needed for bowel control. This is not the standard answer for every cancer labelled stage one.

A pathology review after excision checks the edges and other features. Additional treatment may be recommended if cancer may remain or the findings change the risk assessment. Ask why local surgery, chemoradiotherapy or a combination is recommended for the particular location and tissue type.

Abdominoperineal resection and a permanent colostomy

An abdominoperineal resection, often shortened to APR, removes the anus, rectum and part of the lower colon. It does not mean removal of the abdomen or the entire digestive tract. For anal squamous cancer, it is commonly considered when disease persists or returns after chemoradiotherapy, with other circumstances assessed individually.

Because stool can no longer leave through the anus, the remaining colon is brought to an opening in the abdominal wall called a stoma. Stool collects in a colostomy bag, and the colostomy after APR is permanent. A specialist nurse can explain supplies, skin care and daily life. Discuss recovery, bowel function, urinary or sexual effects and support before surgery.

Advanced or recurrent cancer may need other treatments

Cancer that has spread or cannot be treated with local methods may be managed with systemic medicines, radiotherapy, surgery for selected problems or a clinical trial. The aim may be to control the cancer and relieve symptoms. Immunotherapy is now part of treatment for some patients, but eligibility depends on the exact disease and previous therapy.

For example, the US FDA approved retifanlimab with carboplatin and paclitaxel in 2025 for first-line treatment of adults with inoperable locally recurrent or metastatic anal-canal squamous cancer. It also approved retifanlimab alone after progression on or intolerance to platinum chemotherapy in specified recurrent or metastatic disease. Availability and recommendations differ by country. An oncology team should explain benefits, uncertainties and immune-related risks.

Plan for side effects, support and follow-up

Treatment can cause fatigue, sore skin, diarrhoea, urinary discomfort, nausea or a greater risk of infection. Tell the team early so symptoms can be managed. Obtain its urgent-contact instructions, including the temperature or illness symptoms that require an immediate call. Pain relief and other supportive care can be provided alongside cancer treatment.

If future pregnancy or fertility matters to you, discuss possible effects and preservation options before treatment begins. Ask about sexual wellbeing and practical help at home too. Follow-up continues after treatment to assess recovery, response and possible recurrence; the schedule is individualized. Feeling well does not replace planned checks, and new symptoms should be reported between visits.

Understanding survival figures without treating them as a forecast

US SEER data for diagnoses in 2016–2022 report a five-year relative survival of 70.9% overall, 85.0% for localized disease, 70.1% for regional disease and 36.5% for distant disease. These broad summary categories are not identical to every numbered clinical stage. SEER estimates lifetime diagnosis risk at about 0.2% using 2021–2023 data.

Relative survival compares outcomes with those expected in a similar population without that cancer. It is a group statistic, not an individual life expectancy or a deadline at five years. Tumour features, health, treatment and response all matter, and newer treatments may not be fully represented in older diagnosis cohorts. Ask the treating team what the evidence means for your own situation.

Reducing risk: vaccination, smoking and appropriate follow-up

HPV vaccination prevents new infections with covered types; it does not treat an existing infection or cancer. US CDC guidance recommends routine vaccination at ages 11–12, starting as early as nine, with catch-up through 26. Most people starting before 15 receive two doses; those starting later and immunocompromised people generally need three. Some unvaccinated adults aged 27–45 may benefit after discussion. Local schedules can differ.

Condoms reduce some HPV exposure but cannot cover all potentially infected skin. Appropriate sexual-health care is useful, yet a routine STI test does not guarantee the absence of anal precancer. Avoid tobacco or seek support to stop, keep recommended follow-up for HPV-related disease and discuss risk-based screening with a clinician. No prevention step makes persistent symptoms safe to ignore.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Distinguish benign growths, precancerous surface changes and invasive cancer before choosing treatment.

Chemoradiotherapy is central to care for many anal squamous cancers; screening and vaccination depend on risk and local guidance.

How BeMama can help

Support private, respectful access to care and make room for questions about bowel function, fertility, relationships and practical help during treatment.

When to seek help

Arrange assessment for unexplained bleeding, a persistent lump or changing anal symptoms. Seek emergency care for heavy or ongoing bleeding. During cancer treatment follow the team’s urgent-contact instructions.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Anal cancer is different from a benign lump or precancerous surface change.
  • A biopsy establishes the cancer type; stage and health guide treatment.
  • Many anal squamous cancers are treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy together.
  • Screening is risk-based, and HPV vaccine schedules are not one-size-fits-all.
  • Dated survival figures describe populations, not an individual future.

Frequently asked questions

Are all anal lumps cancer?

No. Many are haemorrhoids, skin tags or other non-cancerous changes. An examination is needed for a persistent or changing lump, and a biopsy may be recommended if its nature is uncertain.

Is AIN the same as invasive cancer?

No. AIN describes abnormal cells confined to the surface lining. Its grade matters: high-grade changes can require treatment or close specialist follow-up to reduce progression risk.

Does HPV always stay forever and cause cancer?

No. Many infections become undetectable without illness. Persistent high-risk infection is the concern, and even that does not make cancer inevitable. Follow the recommended screening and clinical advice.

Can someone develop anal cancer without anal sex?

Yes. A sexual history cannot rule it out. HPV exposure and other risk factors are varied, and symptoms should be assessed without assumptions or blame.

Is an anal Pap test part of ordinary cervical screening?

No. Anal and cervical samples come from different sites. Anal screening is offered through specific risk-based pathways, while symptoms need diagnostic assessment whether or not screening is due.

Is there an effective treatment for anal cancer?

Yes. Many localized anal squamous cancers are treated with curative intent using chemoradiotherapy. Surgery and other medicines have roles in selected situations. The plan depends on type, site, stage and health.

Will treatment always mean a permanent colostomy?

No. Many people receive treatment that preserves the anus. A permanent colostomy is required after an abdominoperineal resection, but that operation is not necessary for every anal cancer.

Does a five-year survival figure tell me how long I will live?

No. It describes outcomes in a group and is not a personal deadline. Your team can interpret prognosis using the cancer’s features, current treatment options and your response.

Does everyone need three HPV vaccine doses?

No. The number depends on the age at the first dose, immune status and local programme. US guidance uses two doses for most people who start before age fifteen, with three in other specified groups.

What should I ask at my first specialist visit?

Ask for the exact pathology and stage, the goal of treatment, why the recommended option fits your case, expected effects on bowel function and fertility, urgent contact instructions and the follow-up plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
